items.stem: A team removes the 'gender' field from training data and declares the model unbiased. Why is this insufficient?

options.text: Other features can act as proxies for gender, so bias can persist despite removing the attribute
options.rationale: Correct: proxy variables reintroduce bias; removal alone is not enough.

options.text: Removing a field always increases bias
options.rationale: It does not always increase bias; the point is removal is insufficient.

options.text: Bias only comes from the model, not data
options.rationale: Bias arises across the lifecycle, including data.
Model capacity is unrelated to proxy bias.

items.explanation: Correct: proxy variables reintroduce bias; removal alone is not enough.

items.stem: Which TWO statements about fairness metrics are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Demographic parity and equalised odds can be mathematically incompatible in general
options.rationale: Correct: fairness impossibility results show common metrics can conflict.

options.text: The appropriate fairness metric depends on the context and the harm of concern
One fairness metric is correct for every situation
options.rationale: No single metric is universally correct.

options.text: A model satisfying one fairness metric satisfies all of them

items.explanation: Correct: fairness impossibility results show common metrics can conflict.

items.stem: A mitigation improves the demographic-parity metric but increases wrongful denials for the group it was meant to help. What does this show?

options.text: Optimising a metric is not the goal; the real-world harm must be evaluated, not just the number
options.rationale: Correct: a metric can improve while actual harm worsens.
The scenario is about metric-vs-harm divergence, not a calculation error.

options.text: Demographic parity is always the right choice
options.rationale: The example shows it can backfire.

options.text: Fairness cannot be measured at all
options.rationale: It can be measured; metrics must be tied to harm.

items.explanation: Correct: a metric can improve while actual harm worsens.
